source: The 400 Investment Banking Interview Questions & Answers You Need to Know

items.prompt_mdx: Accrued Compensation goes up by 10 USD. What happens on the 3 statements (40% tax rate)?

solution.model_answer_mdx: First check that this is a newly recognised expense. If so: operating expenses up 10, Pre-Tax Income down 10, Net Income down **6**. Cash Flow: Net Income down 6, the higher accrued liability adds 10, so operating cash flow and cash are up **4**. Balance Sheet: Cash up 4 on the asset side. On the other side, **Liabilities** up 10 and Retained Earnings down 6, a net 4.

items.prompt_mdx: Inventory goes up by 10 USD and you pay for it with cash. What happens on the 3 statements?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Income Statement: **no change**. Cash Flow Statement: Inventory is an asset, so its increase lowers cash flow from operations by **10**, and the net change in cash is down 10. Balance Sheet: Inventory up 10, **Cash** down 10, so total Assets are unchanged and it still balances.

items.prompt_mdx: Why is the Income Statement not affected by changes in Inventory?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Inventory only becomes an expense when the related goods are **sold**. Until then it sits on the Balance Sheet. It hits **Cost of Goods Sold** at the time of sale. Saying working capital changes appear on the Income Statement is a classic mistake.

items.prompt_mdx: A company orders 10 USD of additional inventory using cash on hand. Nothing has been manufactured or sold yet. What happens on the 3 statements?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Income Statement: **no change**. Cash Flow Statement: Inventory up 10 reduces operating cash flow by **10**, so cash is down 10. Balance Sheet: Inventory up 10, Cash down 10, total Assets unchanged.

items.prompt_mdx: The company now sells those goods for revenue of 20 USD, at a cost of 10 USD. Walk me through the 3 statements (40% tax).

solution.model_answer_mdx: Income Statement: revenue up 20, COGS up 10, so operating income up 10 and Net Income up **6**. Cash Flow Statement: Net Income up 6, and **Inventory** falls by 10, which adds to cash flow, so operating cash flow and cash are up **16**. Balance Sheet: Cash up 16, Inventory down 10, so Assets up 6. Equity up 6.

items.prompt_mdx: What is Working Capital? How is it used?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Working Capital = **Current Assets** minus **Current Liabilities**. Positive means short-term assets cover short-term obligations, so it is read as a soundness indicator. In models bankers prefer **Operating** Working Capital, which strips out cash from current assets and debt from current liabilities.

items.prompt_mdx: What does negative Working Capital mean? Is that a bad sign?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Not necessarily. Subscription or long-contract businesses carry large **Deferred Revenue**, which pushes it negative. Retailers and restaurants are paid **upfront** and can fund payables with that cash, a sign of efficiency. In other cases it does point to financial **trouble**, for instance slow-paying customers combined with heavy debt.

items.prompt_mdx: When would a company collect cash from a customer and not record it as revenue?

solution.model_answer_mdx: When it is paid **upfront** for something it will deliver later: web **subscription** software, mobile carriers selling annual contracts, magazine subscriptions. Under accrual rules revenue is only recorded once the service is **performed**.

items.prompt_mdx: If cash collected is not recorded as revenue, what happens to it?

solution.model_answer_mdx: It goes into **Deferred Revenue**, a **liability** on the Balance Sheet. As the service is delivered, that balance is released into revenue on the Income Statement.

items.prompt_mdx: What is the difference between Accounts Receivable and Deferred Revenue?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Receivables are revenue already recorded but not yet **collected** in cash, an **asset**. Deferred Revenue is cash already collected but not yet recorded as revenue, a **liability**.

items.prompt_mdx: How long does it usually take a company to collect its Accounts Receivable?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Typically around **40** to **50** days. Longer for sellers of high-ticket items, shorter for businesses with small, frequent transactions.

items.prompt_mdx: What is the difference between cash-based and accrual accounting?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Cash-based accounting records revenue and expenses when cash is actually **received** or paid. Accrual accounting records revenue when collection is reasonably certain and expenses when they are **incurred**, whatever the timing of cash. Large companies use accrual. Very small businesses sometimes use cash-based for simplicity.

items.prompt_mdx: A customer pays for a TV with a credit card. How does this look under cash-based versus accrual accounting?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Cash-based: nothing is recorded until the card payment clears and the funds land in the bank, at which point it appears as revenue and as **Cash**. Accrual: revenue is recorded immediately, with the counterpart in **Accounts Receivable**, which converts to Cash once the money arrives.

items.prompt_mdx: How do you decide when to capitalize rather than expense a purchase?

solution.model_answer_mdx: By **useful life**. If the asset serves for more than **1 year** it is capitalised on the Balance Sheet and then **depreciated** (tangible) or amortised (intangible). Factories, equipment and land qualify. Salaries and production costs cover a short period and are expensed.

items.prompt_mdx: Why do companies report both GAAP and non-GAAP (pro forma) earnings?

solution.model_answer_mdx: GAAP income statements carry **non-cash** charges such as amortisation of intangibles, stock-based compensation and deferred revenue write-downs. Companies argue these blur true profitability, so they also publish earnings excluding them, which are almost always **higher**.

items.prompt_mdx: A company has had positive EBITDA for 10 years but recently went bankrupt. How could this happen?

solution.model_answer_mdx: EBITDA ignores several cash drains. Heavy **Capital Expenditures** can make cash flow negative. **Interest** may have become unaffordable. Debt may mature all at once with no way to **refinance** in a credit crunch. Or large **one-time** charges such as litigation can sink it.

items.prompt_mdx: What are examples of non-recurring charges that need to be added back to a company's EBIT or EBITDA?

solution.model_answer_mdx: **Restructuring** charges, goodwill **impairment**, asset write-downs, bad debt expense, legal costs, disaster costs, changes in accounting procedures. To qualify as an add-back, the charge must sit within **Operating Income**. D&A and sometimes stock-based compensation are also added back, but as non-cash items, not as non-recurring ones.

items.prompt_mdx: How do you project Balance Sheet items like Accounts Receivable and Accrued Expenses in a 3-statement model?

solution.model_answer_mdx: With simple ratios held constant or drifting slightly: Accounts Receivable and Deferred Revenue as a **percent** of **revenue**, Accounts Payable as a percent of **COGS**, Accrued Expenses as a percent of operating expenses or SG&A.

items.prompt_mdx: How should you project Depreciation and Capital Expenditures?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Simple way: each as a percentage of **revenue** or of the prior PP&E balance. Detailed way: a **PP&E schedule** that splits assets by useful life, applies straight-line depreciation to each, and bases capex on historical investment levels.
